Crockerland:
{{Short description|Research expedition}}
[[Image:Crocker Land Expedition Members.jpg|thumb|Expedition members. From left to right: Harrison J. Hunt, Maurice C. Tanquary, W. Elmer Ekblaw, Donald B. MacMillan, Fitzhugh Green, and J. L. Allen.]]
[[Image:Bradley Land.jpg|thumb|Alleged locations of Crocker Land, sighted by [[Robert Peary]], and [[Bradley Land]], sighted by [[Frederick Cook]].]]
The '''Crocker Land Expedition''' took place in 1913. Its purpose was to investigate the existence of '''Crocker Land''', a huge island supposedly sighted by the explorer [[Robert Peary]] from the top of [[Cape Colgate]] in 1906. It is now believed that Peary fraudulently invented the island.<ref name=welky>{{cite book|author=David Welky|title=A Wretched and Precarious Situation: In Search of the Last Arctic Frontier|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CtqaCwAAQBAJ&pg=PP1|year=2016|publisher=W. W. Norton|isbn=978-0-393-25442-6}}</ref>

==Background==

Following his 1906 expedition that failed to reach the [[North Pole]], [[Robert Peary|Robert E. Peary]] reported in his book that he had sighted distant land from the heights of the northwestern shore of [[Ellesmere Island]]. He named it Crocker Land, after [[San Francisco]] banker [[George Crocker (businessman)|George Crocker]], one of his [[financial backer]]s. It is now known that Peary's claim was fraudulent,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dioi.org/cot.htm#crck |title=Contributions |author=Rawlins, Dennis |accessdate=2012-12-18 }}</ref> as he wrote in his diary at the time that no land was visible. The invention of Crocker Land was apparently an attempt to secure further support from Crocker for Peary's 1909 expedition. If so, the attempt failed, as Crocker had diverted all of his available resources to the rebuilding of San Francisco following the [[1906 San Francisco earthquake|1906 earthquake]].

The existence or non-existence of Crocker Land became important following the controversial events of the autumn of 1909, when both Peary and [[Frederick Cook]] returned to civilization, claiming to have reached the North Pole. Since Cook claimed to have traversed the alleged region of Crocker Land and found no such land, the existence of Crocker Land would be proof of the falsity of Cook's claim. Backers of Peary's claim therefore set out to find it.

The expedition was organized by [[Donald Baxter MacMillan]] and [[George Borup]], and sponsored by the [[American Museum of Natural History]], the [[American Geographical Society]] and the [[University of Illinois]]' Museum of Natural History.  After Borup's death in 1912, MacMillan took sole control over the expedition.

MacMillan's [[geologist]], [[ornithologist]] and [[botanist]] was [[Walter Elmer Ekblaw]] of the University of Illinois.<ref>{{cite news |title=Doom, death and drama infuse a University of Illinois expedition to the Arctic |url=http://www.uiaa.org/urbana/illinoisalumni/0801b.html |work=[[University of Illinois Alumni Association]] |accessdate=2009-07-23 |archive-date=2009-02-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090211223137/http://uiaa.org/urbana/illinoisalumni/0801b.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Dr. Ekblaw, Once Arctic Explorer For U. of I., Dies |url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/chicagotribune/access/489278102.html?dids=489278102:489278102&FMT=CITE&FMTS=CITE:AI&date=Jun+07%2C+1949&author=&pub=Chicago+Tribune&desc=DR.+EKBLAW%2C+ONCE+ARCTIC+EXPLORER+FOR+U.+OF+I.%2C+DIES&pqatl=google |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021161022/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/chicagotribune/access/489278102.html?dids=489278102:489278102&FMT=CITE&FMTS=CITE:AI&date=Jun+07,+1949&author=&pub=Chicago+Tribune&desc=DR.+EKBLAW,+ONCE+ARCTIC+EXPLORER+FOR+U.+OF+I.,+DIES&pqatl=google |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 21, 2012 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=June 7, 1949 |accessdate=2009-07-23 }}</ref> [[United States Navy|Navy]] [[Ensign (rank)|Ensign]] [[Fitzhugh Green, Sr.|Fitzhugh Green]] served as [[engineer]] and [[physicist]]. [[Maurice Cole Tanquary]], of the University of Illinois, was the [[zoologist]], and [[Harrison J. Hunt]] the surgeon.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://entohistory.tamu.edu/hallofhonor/hallofhonor.html |title=Maurice C. Tanquary |accessdate=2009-07-24|publisher=[[Texas A&M University]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100625234845/http://entohistory.tamu.edu/hallofhonor/hallofhonor.html |archive-date=2010-06-25 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Dr. M.C. Tanquary, Entomologist, 62. Minnesota Professor, Pioneer in Modern Beekeeping, Dies. Served With MacMillan. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1944/10/26/archives/dr-m-3-tahquary-entomologist-62-minnesota-professor-pioneer-in.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 26, 1944 |accessdate=2009-07-24 }}</ref>

[[Image:Minik in New York.jpg|thumb|upright|Minik Wallace as a child]]
[[Minik Wallace]], the [[Inuk]] brought to the [[United States]] as a child by Robert Peary in 1897, was the guide and translator for the expedition.<ref>[http://www.spurlock.uiuc.edu/collections/browse/crockerland/crockerland_txt.html Spurlock Museum] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080827222607/http://www.spurlock.uiuc.edu/collections/browse/crockerland/crockerland_txt.html |date=2008-08-27 }}</ref>

As well as confirming and mapping the position of Crocker Land, the declared purpose of the expedition was to investigate "[[geology]], [[geography]], [[glaciology]], [[meteorology]], [[terrestrial magnetism]], [[electrical phenomena]], [[seismology]], [[zoology]] (both [[Vertebrata|vertebrate]] and [[Invertebrata|invertebrate]]), [[botany]], [[oceanography]], [[ethnology]], and [[archaeology]]".

In newspapers of the time, MacMillan described Crocker Land as "the world’s last geographical problem".

{{Blockquote|text=In June 1906, Commander Peary, from the summit of Cape Thomas Hubbard, at about [[83rd parallel north|latitude 83 degrees N]], [[100th meridian west|longitude 100 degrees W]], reported seeing land glimmering in the northwest, approximately {{convert|130|mi|km|disp=sqbr}} away across the [[Arctic Ocean|Polar Sea]]. He did not go there, but he gave it a name in honor of the late George Crocker of the Peary Arctic Club. That is Crocker Land. Its boundaries and extent can only be guessed at, but I am certain that strange animals will be found there, and I hope to discover a new race of men.}}

==The expedition==
The expedition left [[Brooklyn Navy Yard]] aboard the steamer ''Diana'' on 2 July 1913.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.uiaa.org/urbana/illinoisalumni/0108_b.html |title=University of Illinois |access-date=2008-02-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204050952/http://www.uiaa.org/urbana/illinoisalumni/0108_b.html |archive-date=2008-12-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Two weeks later, at midnight on 16 July, the ''Diana'' struck rocks while trying to avoid an [[iceberg]]. MacMillan blamed the collision on the captain, who was drunk at the time. The expedition transferred to another ship, the ''Erik'', and eventually arrived at [[Etah, Greenland|Etah]], in north-west [[Greenland]], on the second week of August.

The next three weeks were spent constructing a large eight-room shed, with electricity generation capabilities, that was to serve as the local headquarters of the expedition. An attempt was also made to set up a radio room, but it was not successful, and the expedition was never able to establish reliable radio communications with the outside world.

After making a number of preliminary trips to place supply caches along the route, MacMillan, Green, Ekblaw and seven [[Inuit]] set off on the {{convert|1200|mi|km|adj=on}} journey to Crocker Land on 11 March 1914. The temperature was many degrees below zero and weather conditions were very poor.

Eventually, the party reached the {{convert|4700|ft|m|adj=mid|-high}} [[Beitstadt Glacier]], which took them three days to climb. The temperature dropped dramatically and Ekblaw suffered severe [[frostbite]]. He was evacuated back to Etah by some of the Inuit.

One by one, the other members of the party gave up and turned back. By the time the expedition reached the edge of the [[Arctic Ocean]] on 11 April, only MacMillan, Green and two Inuit, Piugaattoq and Ittukusuk, remained. The four dog sleds set off across the treacherous sea ice, avoiding thin patches and expanses of open water, and eventually, on 21 April, the party saw what appeared to be a huge island on the north-western horizon. As MacMillan later said, "Hills, valleys, snow-capped peaks extending through at least one hundred and twenty degrees of the horizon.”

Piugaattoq, an Inuk hunter with 20 years of experience of the area, explained that it was just an [[illusion]]. He called it ''poo-jok'', which means '[[mist]]'. However, MacMillan insisted they press on, even though it was late in the season and the sea ice was breaking up. For five days they went on, following the mirage. Finally, on 27 April, after they had covered some {{convert|125|mi|km}} of dangerous sea ice, MacMillan was forced to admit that Piugaattoq was right—the land that they had sighted was in fact a mirage. (It was probably a rare form of mirage called a [[Fata Morgana (mirage)|Fata Morgana]].)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mirages and Green Flashes |url=https://aty.sdsu.edu/mirages/mirintro.html |access-date=2025-10-26 |website=aty.sdsu.edu |language=en-US}}</ref>

Later MacMillan wrote:

{{Blockquote|The day was exceptionally clear, not a cloud or trace of mist; if land could be seen, now was our time. Yes, there it was! It could even be seen without a glass, extending from southwest true to north-northeast. Our powerful glasses, however, brought out more clearly the dark background in contrast with the white, the whole resembling hills, valleys and snow-capped peaks to such a degree that, had we not been out on the frozen sea for 150 miles, we would have staked our lives upon its reality. Our judgment then, as now, is that this was a mirage or loom of the sea ice.|title=from ''Four Years in the White North''<ref name="Four Years in the White North">{{cite book|last1=MacMillan|first1=Donald Baxter|last2=Ekblaw|first2=Walter Elmer|title=Four Years in the White North|date=1918|publisher=Harper & Brothers|pages=87–88|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gkUNAQAAIAAJ&q=MIRAGE+LOOM|accessdate=25 March 2018}}</ref>}}

The party turned around and was able to reach solid land—with no time to spare, for the sea ice broke up the next day.<ref>[http://www.provincetownbanner.com/article/_/26035/History/4/18/2002 The Province Town Banner (7 Feb 2008)]</ref>

==The killing of Piugaattoq==
After returning to land, MacMillan sent Piugaattoq and Green to explore a route to the west. The weather turned against them and they were forced to take shelter in a [[snow cave]]. One of the dog teams died in the snow, and during a squabble<ref name="nunatsiaq/taissumani-1914" /> over which direction to travel next, Green took a rifle from the sled and shot Piugaattoq in the back, killing him.<ref name=welky/><ref>{{cite web |last1=Schmidt |first1=Kim |title=Mirage & Murder in the Arctic |url=https://storied.illinois.edu/crocker-land/ |website=Storied |publisher=University of Illinois |date=April 21, 2017}}</ref>

On 4 May Green rejoined MacMillan and told him what had happened. Upon their return to Etah, MacMillan informed the other American members of the expedition, but asked them to keep quiet. He told the Inuit that Piugaattoq had died in an avalanche. Ekblaw said later that this was "one of the darkest and most deplorable tragedies in the annals of Arctic exploration."

Green was never prosecuted for the murder, although the Inuit suspected there was more to the story than had been told and that Green had had a relationship with Piugaattoq's wife [[Aleqasina]]<ref name="hoiem.illinois.edu/crocker-peary">{{cite web |last1=Hoiem |first1=Elizabeth Massa |title=Peary family · Inuit in Children's Books about Arctic Expeditions |url=https://www.hoiem.web.illinois.edu/dir/exhibits/show/inuit-arctic-expeditions/crocker-expedition/peary-family |website=www.hoiem.web.illinois.edu |access-date=16 August 2026}}</ref><ref name="978-1-5107-2638-3">{{cite book |last1=Counter |first1=S. Allen |title=North Pole Legacy: The Search for the Arctic Offspring of Robert Peary and Matthew Henson |date=13 February 2018 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=978-1-5107-2638-3 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="nunatsiaq/SnowBaby">{{cite news |last1=Harper |first1=Kenn |title=The women in Peary's life The Snow Baby” |url=https://nunatsiaq.com/stories/article/The_women_in_Pearys_life_The_Snow_Baby/ |access-date=16 August 2026 |work=[[Nunatsiaq News]] |language=en |quote=Taissumani is an occasional column that recalls events of historical interest. ==The return home==
The expedition attempted to head for home, but the weather turned against them and they were stranded in the region for the next four months.

In December 1914, MacMillan and Tanquary set off for Etah with the intention of sending a message to the outside world that a rescue was needed the following summer. They quickly ran into trouble with the weather, and MacMillan turned back. Tanquary pressed on and eventually reached Etah in mid-March 1915.

Word reached the American Museum of Natural History. That summer, the ''George B. Cluett'', a three-masted schooner completely unsuitable for Arctic waters, was sent, captained by [[George Comer]]. The vessel never reached the expedition. It ended up trapped in ice and did not return for two years.<ref name="ucalgary">{{cite web |url=http://pubs.aina.ucalgary.ca/arctic/Arctic36-3-294.pdf |title=George Comer |last=Ross |first=W. Gillies |work=Arctic Profiles |pages=294–295 |publisher=ucalgary.ca |accessdate=2008-03-30 |archive-date=2016-03-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303180447/http://pubs.aina.ucalgary.ca/arctic/Arctic36-3-294.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 1916, a second relief ship was sent, and ran into similar problems. By this time, Tanquary, Green and Allen had made their own way back to the United States by dog sled.

The rest of the expedition was eventually rescued in 1917 by the ship ''Neptune'', commanded by Captain [[Robert Bartlett (explorer)|Robert Bartlett]].<ref>Four Years in the White North. Bartlett</ref>

==Aftermath==
[[Image:UIUC spurlock.JPG|thumb|upright|Spurlock Museum]]

Although the expedition failed to map the non-existent Crocker Land, much important research was done. A considerable number of photographs and artifacts were brought back, documenting the indigenous peoples and natural habitat of the region.

Hundreds of photos of the expedition and over 200 artifacts are displayed in the University of Illinois' [[Spurlock Museum]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.spurlock.uiuc.edu/index.html |title=Spurlock Museum, U of I |publisher=Spurlock.uiuc.edu |accessdate=2017-05-12}}</ref> There is also a permanent exhibit at the Peary–MacMillan Arctic Museum on the grounds of [[Bowdoin College]] in Brunswick, Maine.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bowdoin.edu/arctic-museum/ |title=Bowdoin College Peary MacMillan Arctic Museum |publisher=Bowdoin.edu |accessdate=2017-05-12}}</ref> Journals from Tanquary, Ekblaw and Donald MacMillan and his wife Miriam are available online at the George J. Mitchell Department of Special Collections & Archives website.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://library.bowdoin.edu/arch/index.shtml|title=George J. Mitchell Department of Special Collections & Archives (Bowdoin Library - George J. Mitchell Department of Special Collections & Archives)|website=library.bowdoin.edu|access-date=2016-11-16}}</ref> Digitization of materials at Bowdoin College related to the Crocker Land Expedition was funded by the Gladys Krieble Delmas Foundation in November 2015.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://nationtalk.ca/story/arctic-museum-receives-grant-to-digitize-hundred-year-old-collection|title=Arctic Museum Receives Grant to Digitize Hundred-Year-Old Collection|website=Atlantic NationTalk|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-11}}</ref>

Tuanaki:
{{Short description|Islets once part of the Cook Islands}}

[[File:Stielers Handatlas 1891 76 Cook detail.png|thumb]]
'''Tuanaki''' or '''Tuanahe''' is the name of an [[anecdotal]] vanished group of islets, once part of the [[Cook Islands]]. It was located south of [[Rarotonga]]<ref>[[Elsdon Best|Best, Elsdon]] (1923). ''[https://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-BesPoly-t1-body-d1-d4.html#n10 Polynesian Voyagers. the Maori as a Deep-Sea Navigator, Explorer, and Colonizer]''. Wellington: [[Dominion Museum]]. New Zealand Texts Collection.</ref> and within two days sail of [[Mangaia]].<ref>{{cite book | last = Ramsay | first = Raymond | title = No Longer on the Map | publisher = Viking Press | location = New York | year = 1972 | isbn = 0-670-51433-0 | page =213 }}</ref>

In 1916, the [[Polynesian Society of Honolulu]] reprinted an account by a sailor who had visited there in 1842, spending six days among the natives.  However this account added that two years later in 1844, a schooner of English missionaries had found nothing.<ref>{{cite book |last=Gill |first=William Wyatt |author-link=William Wyatt Gill |author2=Stephenson Percy Smith  |title=Rarotonga Records: Being Extracts from the Papers of the Late Rev. W. Wyatt Gill |publisher=The Polynesian Society |year=1916 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/rarotongarecord00smitgoog/page/n35 29]–31 |url=https://archive.org/details/rarotongarecord00smitgoog }}</ref>  Some Tuanakians who had emigrated to Rarotonga allegedly survived.

The 1916 publication re-ignited interest in the flyaway islands, and explorer Sir [[Ernest Shackleton]], when planning the [[Shackleton–Rowett Expedition]] of 1921–1922, proclaimed as one of his goals the rediscovery of Tuanaki.  The explorer died in Antarctic waters before he was able to mount a serious search for the vanished archipelago.<ref name="Spokesman-Review">{{cite web |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=FrFXAAAAIBAJ&sjid=uPMDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6442,621950 |title=Shackleton, Antarctic Explorer, is Dead |work=[[The Spokesman-Review|The (Spokane) Spokesman-Review]] |date=February 3, 1922 |access-date=17 March 2012}}</ref>

It was suggested in 1952 that the [[Haymet Rocks]] were a remnant of Tuanaki.<ref>{{Citation | title=THE MYSTERY OF TUANAKI ISLAND | journal=[[Pacific Islands Monthly]] | publication-date=1952-02-01 | volume=xxii | issue=7 | pages=104 | issn=0030-8722 }}</ref> However, the existence of the Haymet Rocks at some point is unconfirmed as well.

== Tuanaki in art ==

The band [[Beirut (band)|Beirut]] titled one of the songs from their seventh album, ''A Study of Losses'', released in 2025, in reference to Tuanaki Island, ''Tuanaki Atoll''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Beirut Pays Tribute to a South Pacific Eden on New Single “Tuanaki Atoll” |url=https://floodmagazine.com/189883/listen-beirut-tuanaki-atoll/ |access-date=23 March 2025 |website=[[Flood Magazine]]}}</ref>

'''Ganges Island''', a [[phantom island]] known as {{nihongo||中ノ鳥島 or 中鳥島|Nakanotorishima|literally "central bird island"}} in Japanese, appeared at  on maps of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.<ref>{{cite book | last = Stommel | first = Henry | title = Lost Islands: The Story of Islands That Have Vanished from Nautical Charts | publisher = University of British Columbia Press | location = Vancouver | year = 1984 | isbn = 0-7748-0210-3 | pages = xvii, 132 | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/lostislands00henr }}</ref>  Reports of its disappearance appeared in 1933.<ref>[http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19330712-1.2.100.aspx "Island in Pacific Vanishes".] ''[[The Straits Times]]''. 12 July 1933. p. 12.</ref>

The purported island was considered a part of an [[Anson Archipelago]], which included other phantom islands such as [[Los Jardines]] as well as real islands such as [[Wake Island|Wake]] and [[Marcus Island]]s.

== History ==
=== ''Discovery'' by Americans ===
Ganges Island is probably named after the ship [[Ganges (1809 whaler)|Ganges]], a Nantucket whaler active in the Pacific between 1815 and 1851, which discovered several islands in the Pacific. The discovery may have taken place during one of the ship's first three campaigns: August 1815 to October 1817 (Captain Isaiah Ray), June 1818 to June 1821 (Captain Isaiah Ray) or August 1821 to March 1824 (Captain [[Coffin (whaling family)|Joshua Coffin]]).<ref name=star>{{Cite book|url=|title=History Of The American Whale Fishery: From Its Earliest Inception To The Year 1876|author=Alexander Starbuck|year=2015|publisher=Scholar's Choice|isbn=9781295950089}}</ref>

Ganges Island is referenced in 1826 on ''[[Bowditch's American Practical Navigator]]'' at position: {{Coord|30|45|N|154|25|E}}, then on a map of 1832. In 1841, [[Jeremiah N. Reynolds]] attributed the same position to Ganges Island, noting a nearby island: {{Coord|31|N|155|E}}, which he believed to be the same island.,<ref name=reynolds203/> but also another position of nearby Ganges Island {{Coord|31|00|N|154|10|E}}.<ref name=reynolds204/> Similarly, [[Alexander George Findlay]]'s book lists two sightings at {{Coord|31|30|N|154|0|E}} and {{Coord|31|30|N|163|0|E}} as being the same as the "Ganges Reef" at {{Coord|30|47|N|154|20|E}}, itself presented as "doubtful."<ref name=fin/>

From its first mention in 1826, Ganges Island remained in ''Bowditch's American Practical Navigator'' until 1880, but disappeared in 1888. In 1875, a major revision of the U.S. Admiralty removed many dubious islands, including Ganges Island, from the charts, but continued to record various reefs in the area until 1941.

===''Rediscovery'' by Japanese===
The Japanese government also had this information.<ref name=hiraoka2008 /> The ''Japan Hydrographic Magazine'' in 1904 by the then Japanese [[Ministry of the Navy (Japan)|Ministry of the Navy]] Hydrographic Department also states that;
: Ogasawara Islanders have explored it several times in the past but failed to find it. It is listed on nautical charts as ''P.D.'' (Position Doubtful.) Its presence or absence has not yet been determined, so voyagers should exercise extreme caution. 
The coordinates of Ganges Island, {{Coord|30|47|N|154|15|E|name=Ganges Island}}, {{Coord|30|47|N|154|16|E|name=Ganges Reef}}, etc. were then marked.<ref>{{Cite book | title=日本水路誌 |volume=第一巻 |edition=第一改版 |publisher=水路部|date=1904-12-28 |page=344 |doi=10.11501/10304285 |author1=海軍省水路部 }}</ref>

[[File:中ノ鳥島.gif |thumb|Teizaburo Yamada reported ''Ganges Island'']]

In August 1907, Teizaburo Yamada of [[Tokyo City]] reported that he had discovered [[Islands]] 560 [[Nautical mile]]s from [[Ogasawara Islands]], and had [[Geographical exploration|explored]] and [[Surveying|surveyed]]. The report was submitted to the [[Ogasawara Subprefecture]] on April 28, 1908, in which Yamada compared the island he had discovered to "Ganges Island" and submitted it with a "Notification of Discovery of Islands Belonging to Ogasawara Island" and a map of the island.<ref name=hiraoka2008 />

According to the " Notification of Discovery of Islands Belonging to Ogasawara Island ", the island was located at {{Coord|30|05|N|154|02|E}}. The island has a circumference of 1[[Li (unit)|ri]] 25 cho (about 6.67  [[Kilometre|km]]), an area of 643,700 [[Pyeong|tsubo]] (about 2.13  [[Square kilometre|km<sup>2</sup>]]), and some [[vegetation]], which appeared to be [[coral reef]]s. The island was also covered with [[phosphorite]], which is formed when [[guano]] accumulates, and was considered important at the time as a [[gunpowder]] material and [[fertilizer]].

Yamada's report of the discovery contains a number of oddities, including the fact that the location of the island does not correspond to the distance from the island to the Ogasawara Islands, and that there were several million albatrosses there even though [[short-tailed albatross|albatross]] did not fly there at that time of year.{{Sfn|Hiraoka|2012|p=91}}

Based on Yamada's report, Hiroshi Abe, the Governor of Tokyo Prefecture, submitted a "Report on the New Island Administrative District Allocation" to the Minister of Home Affairs, [[Takashi Hara]], along with a "Notification of the Discovery of Islands Belonging to Ogasawara Island".

On July 22, 1908, Named "Nakanotori Island" and incorporated into Japanese territory by Japanese Cabinet decision.<ref name="編入">「[https://www.digital.archives.go.jp/DAS/meta/listPhoto?KEYWORD=&LANG=jpn&BID=F0000000000000006208&ID=M0000000000001745523&NO= 東京府小笠原島ヲ距ル五百六十哩ノ位置ニ在ル無人島ヲ中ノ鳥島ト名ケ東京府小笠原島庁ノ所管トス] 」『公文類聚・第三十二編』、[https://www.digital.archives.go.jp/ 国立公文書館デジタルアーカイブ]</ref> According to the minutes of the Cabinet meeting, the island discovered by Yamada was reported to correspond to "Ganges Island" on the nautical charts, but since it was different from the location of Ganges Island in ''Japan Hydrographic Magazine'', it was necessary to determine the location at a later date, saying "There is a slight difference in its location, and it is necessary to determine it on another day." However, it was also stated that "there is no argument that it belongs to Japanese territory."

=== Failure of large-scale surveys===
[[File:最近太平洋地圖_中ノ鳥島.png|thumb|Nakanotorishima (島鳥ノ中) on a 1941 map of Japan (center right)]]

However, Nakanotori Island has not been found again since.<ref>{{Cite journal  |author=長谷川亮一 |url=https://opac.ll.chiba-u.jp/da/curator/100320/ |title=「中ノ鳥島」の探検者・大平三次の伝記のための覚書 : 自由民権活動家から投機的実業化へ |journal=千葉大学大学院人文社会科学研究科研究プロジェクト報告書 |volume=第296集 |publisher=千葉大学大学院 |date=2016-02-28 |pages=2–14}}</ref> Especially in the [[Taisho era]] (1912–1926), the surrounding waters were explored on a large scale, but no discovery was made at all. In 1913, the "Yoshioka Maru" went to survey Nakanotori Island, but failed to find the island.{{Sfn|Hiraoka|2012|p=90}}

In September 1927, a survey was conducted by the [[Aviso]] "Manshu", but the island was not found.{{Sfn|Hiraoka|2012|pp=91-92}} Thus, it was removed from the [[Imperial Japanese Navy|Japanese Navy]]'s classified hydrographic charts by the Naval Hydrographic Notification of 1943, along with Ganges Reef, as it was implicitly not real.

===After WWII===
On January 29, 1946, after World War II, the [[Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers|General Headquarters of the Allied Powers]] issued Instruction No. 677 on the scope of "Japan."<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.hoppou.go.jp/library/document/data/19460129.html |title=連合軍最高司令部訓令（SCAPIN）第677号 |publisher=[[Independent Administrative Institution|独立行政法人]]北方領土問題対策協会|accessdate=2007-07-27 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20060628201837/http://www.hoppou.go.jp/library/document/data/19460129.html |archivedate=2006-06-28}}</ref> Although it stated that this "means the extent of Japan for the purpose of this Instruction and does not indicate the extent of Japanese territory," the following list, including "Nakanotori-shimaNakanotorishima" was presented.
: (a)[[Ulleungdo]], [[Liancourt Rocks]], [[Jeju Island]]; (b) All other islands of the Outer Pacific, including [[Ryukyu Islands]] south of 30 degrees north latitude (include [[Kuchinoshima]]), [[Izu Islands]], [[South Seas Mandate]], Ogasawara, Iwo Islands, [[Daitō Islands]], [[Okinotorishima]], [[Minamitorishima]], '''Nakanotorishima;''' (c) [[Kuril Islands]], [[Habomai Islands]] (include [[Tanfiliev Island]], [[Yuri (island)|Yuri]], [[Anuchina]], [[Zelyony Island (Kuril Islands)|Zelyony Island]], [[Polonsky Island]]), [[Shikotan]].

On November 22, 1946, Japanese [[Ministry of Transport (Japan)|Ministry of Transport]]'s Hydrographic Department issued Notice No. 46, stating that "The reefs suspected to be located approximately 14 nautical miles north of Nakanotorishima Island and the island were found not to exist as a result of a precise survey" and were deleted from general hydrographic publications.<ref>{{Cite journal  |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/2962473/1/8 |title=水路告示第46号 |journal=[[Kanpō (Japanese government gazette)|官報]] |issue=5959 |publisher=大蔵省 [[National Printing Bureau|印刷局]] |date=1946-11-12 |pages=183 |doi=10.11501/2962473 |author1=大蔵省印刷局 }}</ref>

Although the description of Nakanotori Island was deleted sequentially in accordance with the public notice, unamended hydrographic charts and maps were still circulated in the private sector, such as those depicted in the "Koutou Shinchizu" (高等新地図) published in 1953.<ref>{{Cite news |author=安藤健二 |url=https://www.huffingtonpost.jp/entry/ganges-island_jp_619b0fb5e4b0ae9a42a2ac84 |title=中ノ鳥島とは？ 実在しない島を日本領に編入。海図から削除されて75年 |newspaper=[[HuffPost]] |date=2021-11-22|access-date=2023-12-23}}</ref>

At a House of Councilors General Affairs Committee meeting on April 7, 1998, [[Chief Cabinet Secretary]] Kenzo Muraoka responded to a question about Nakanotorishima: 
:In July 1908, the Cabinet made a decision to "name the island Nakanotorishima and to place it under the jurisdiction of the Ogasawara Islands Agency in Tokyo Prefecture." In 1943, "it was deleted from the Confidential Hydrographic Chart" and in 1946, "Nakanotorishima does not exist," " Detailed observations have shown that it does not exist." Therefore, the existence of Nakanotorishima is not currently confirmed.<ref>{{Cite web
| title =第142回国会 参議院 総務委員会 第7号 平成10年4月7日|publisher=[[National Diet Library|国立国会図書館]]|website=国会会議録検索システム

| url = https://kokkai.ndl.go.jp/#/detail?minId=114214601X00719980407&spkNum=79&current=1
| date = 1998-04-07 |accessdate=2014-08-08
| author = [[Chief Cabinet Secretary]]村岡兼造村岡兼造}}</ref>

Rivadeneyra Shoal:
{{Short description|Shoal in the Eastern Pacific Ocean}}
[[File:Stielers Handatlas 1891 76.jpg|thumb|1891 German map showing Rivadeneyra Shoal.]]
'''Rivadeneyra Shoal''' is a [[shoal]] or [[seamount]] in the [[Eastern Pacific Ocean]] between [[Malpelo Island]] and [[Cocos Island]]. It was reported in October 1842 at the position {{coord|4|15|N|85|10|W|display=inline,title}} with a depth of 10 feet.  It was unsuccessfully searched for by the British war vessels {{HMS|Cockatrice|1832|6}} and {{HMS|Havannah|1811|6}} in 1854 and 1857 respectively, and by the {{USS|Mohican|1883|6}} in 1885.

Pactolus Bank:
{{short description|Unconfirmed undersea bank in the southern Pacific Ocean}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2020}}
'''Pactolus Bank''' (or '''Burnham Bank''') is (or was) a [[seamount]] in the [[Southern Ocean]], west of [[Cape Horn]]. It was discovered by Captain W.D. Burnham of the American ship ''Pactolus'' on November 6, 1885.
The bank has been proposed as a possible location for [[Elizabeth Island (Cape Horn)|Elizabeth Island]], a [[phantom island]] reported by [[Sir Francis Drake]] in October 1578. However, subsequent surveys have been unable to locate the bank, which may itself be a phantom.

==Discovery==
Burnham reported to the [[Hydrographic Office#United States|US Hydrographic Office]] that "while running before a gale off [[Cape Horn]] in command of the American ship ''Pactolus'' at 4 o'clock in the morning of 6 November 1885, the wind lulled and the sea fell, and noticing very highly discoloured water, he hove the ship to and [[Sound (nautical)|sounded]] three times, obtaining each time from 67 to 70 [[fathom|fms]]. of black sand and small rocks". He then "ran South for 30 miles before the water, which all the time was very thick and yellow, resumed its natural colour". He reports "the line of demarcation was very distinct".<ref>USHO 1938; quoted in Riesenberg p65-66</ref> Burnham gives the position of the soundings as {{coord|56|36|S|74|20|W|display=inline}}. He states that an English ship from [[San Francisco]] to [[Liverpool]] reported discoloured water in the same location at the same time.<ref>Riesenberg p65-66</ref>

Marine historian [[Felix Riesenberg]] notes that earlier mariners had observed large icebergs stationary in the area, suggesting they had grounded on the bank; these have typically been 200 ft or more in height, with a corresponding depth of 800 to 1,400 ft below the surface;<ref>Riesenberg p207</ref> others could have been several miles in length and up to 1000 ft high, while an iceberg sighted by a Captain CC Dixon in 1860 was L-shaped, 50 miles long on one leg, and 30 miles on the other.<ref>Riesenberg p208</ref> These icebergs have been observed stationary for up to a month in the vicinity of the bank, and are thought to be responsible for the loss of several ships that have run into them, or been trapped.<ref>Riesenberg p207-8</ref>

==Significance==
Felix Riesenberg, who served under Burnham, postulated that Pactolus Bank was the sunken location of [[Elizabeth Island (Cape Horn)|Elizabeth Island]], discovered by [[Francis Drake|Sir Francis Drake]]'s ship the ''[[Golden Hinde]]'' in 1578. Leaving the [[Magellan Strait]], Drake's ship was driven far to the west and south, before clawing its way back towards land. On 22 October the ship anchored off an island which Drake, according to Riesenberg, named "Elizabeth Island", where wood and water was collected and seals and penguins captured for food, along with "herbs of great virtue". According to Drake's Portuguese pilot, [[Nuno da Silva (navigator)|Nuno da Silva]], their position at the anchorage was 57°S. However, no island has been confirmed at that latitude, although a sinking volcanic island may have been sighted in that vicinity by the Danish ship ''Lutterfeld'' in December 1876 or 1877.{{citation needed|date=May 2020}}

Historian [[Mateo Martinic]], however, considers [[Sars Bank]], 350 km south of [[Diego Ramírez Islands]], as a better fit for Elizabeth Island.<ref name=Martinic2019>{{cite journal |last1=Martinic B.|first1=Mateo |author-link1=Mateo Martinic |date=2019 |title=Entre el mito y la realidad. La situación de la misteriosa Isla Elizabeth de Francis Drake|trans-title=Between myth and reality. The situation of the mysterious Elizabeth Island of Francis Drake |url=https://scielo.conicyt.cl/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0718-22442019000100005&lng=es&nrm=iso&tlng=es |journal=[[Magallania]] |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=5–14 |doi=10.4067/S0718-22442019000100005 |access-date=December 21, 2019| language=es |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Fate==
{{Unreferenced section|date=February 2021}}
The [[Bear of Oakland|USS ''Bear'' (AG-29)]] investigated the area in March 1940, but her log does not mention any soundings or results. The {{USS|Wyandot | AKA-92}} investigated the area in 1956 and found no indication of a shoal.
The importance of these attempts is extremely limited,{{Clarify|reason=|date=February 2021}} mainly due to the severe weather these ships had to operate in. Therefore, Pactolus Bank may itself be a [[phantom island]].

In 2008, Dutchman Hylke Tromp, after some years of research, published a comprehensive report, containing all known facts and myths regarding the Pactolus Bank.

New South Greenland:
{{short description|Antarctic island previously believed to exist}}
[[Image:New South Greenland Map.png|thumb|300px|alt= Chart shows the positions of the supposed New South Greenland coast, and Ross's Appearance, in relation to the Antarctic peninsula, the South American mainland, the South Sandwich Islands and South Georgia.|Map showing Morrell's reported location of the "New South Greenland" coast (1823, red line), and "Ross's Appearance" as reported by Sir James Clark Ross in 1841. The dotted line indicates the area of Captain Johnson's 1821 voyage.]]

'''New South Greenland''', sometimes known as '''Morrell's Land''', was an [[phantom island|appearance of land]] recorded by the American captain [[Benjamin Morrell]] of the [[schooner]] ''Wasp'' in {{Nowrap|March 1823}}, during a [[seal hunting|sealing]] and exploration voyage in the [[Weddell Sea]] area of Antarctica. Morrell provided precise coordinates and a description of a coastline which he claimed to have sailed along for more than {{convert|300|mi|-2}}. Because the Weddell Sea area was so little visited and hard to navigate due to ice conditions, the alleged land was never properly investigated before its existence was emphatically disproven during Antarctic expeditions in the early 20th century.

At the time of Morrell's voyage, the geography of the then-unnamed Weddell Sea and its surrounding coasts was almost entirely unknown, making the claimed sighting initially plausible. However, obvious errors in Morrell's voyage account and his general reputation as a [[Fable|fabulist]] created scepticism about the existence of this new land. In {{Nowrap|June 1912}}, the German explorer [[Wilhelm Filchner]] searched for but found no traces of land after his ship ''Deutschland'' became icebound in the Weddell Sea and drifted into the locality of Morrell's observation. A [[sounding line|line sounding]] of the sea bottom revealed more than {{convert|5000|ft|m|sigfig=2}} of water, indicating no land in near proximity. Three years later, trapped in the same waters with his ship [[Endurance (1912 ship)|''Endurance'']], [[Ernest Shackleton]] was able by similar means to confirm the land's implausibility.

Various explanations for Morrell's error have been suggested, including intentional deception. However, Morrell describes his find briefly and prosaically, evidently seeking no personal credit or glory from the discovery. In his narrative, he assigns the honour to his fellow sealing captain, Robert Johnson, for finding and naming the land two years earlier. Morrell may have been honestly mistaken, through miscalculation of his ship's position (the reported coastline does roughly match the shape of the nearest real one, but offset by a large distance) or by misremembering detail when writing the account after nine years. Alternatively, he may have made the common error of confusing distant icebergs with land, or been misled by the distorting effects of [[Fata Morgana (mirage)|Antarctic mirage]]. In 1843, British naval explorer [[James Clark Ross]] reported possible land in a position close to Morrell's; this land, too, would eventually be proven not to exist.

== Voyage of the ''Wasp'', 1822–23 ==

===  June 1822 to March 1823 ===
In the early 19th century, the geography of Antarctica was almost completely unknown, though occasional sightings of land had been recorded.<ref>For details of early Antarctic land sightings, including [[Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen|Bellingshausen]]'s first sighting of the Antarctic mainland,  see Headland, pp. 108–30</ref> In 1822, Benjamin Morrell, who had sailed to the [[South Sandwich Islands]] the previous year,<ref>Morrell, pp. xx to xxvii</ref> was appointed commander of the schooner ''Wasp'' for a two-year voyage of sealing, trading and exploration in the Antarctic seas and the southern [[Pacific Ocean]].<ref name= preface>Morrell, p. xxvii</ref> In addition to his sealing duties, Morrell had, as he put it, "discretionary powers to prosecute new discoveries."<ref name= preface/> He proposed to use this discretion to investigate the Antarctic seas "and to ascertain the practicality ... of penetrating to the [[South Pole]]."<ref name= preface/> This would be the first of four extended voyages that would keep Morrell at sea for most of the following eight years, although he would not revisit the Antarctic after the initial voyage.<ref>The subsequent voyages, in successive ships, would take Morrell to the Pacific Ocean, the south and west coasts of Africa, and the Indian Ocean. See Morrell, Contents pages i to vii</ref>

''Wasp'' sailed south from New York on {{Nowrap|22 June}} 1822. She reached the [[Falkland Islands]] late in October, after which Morrell spent 16 days in fruitless searches for the nonexistent [[Aurora Islands]],<ref>The Aurora Islands were one of numerous [[phantom islands]] reported in sub-Antarctic waters, eventually proved to be nonexistent. See list of phantom sightings in {{cite web|title= Non-existent islands (in Summary of Peri-Antarctic Islands)|url= http://www.spri.cam.ac.uk/resources/infosheets/19.html|publisher= Scott Polar Research Institute|year= 1996|access-date= 17 December 2008}}.</ref><ref name= WJM>W.J Mills, pp.  434–35</ref> before heading for [[South Georgia]], where the ship anchored on {{Nowrap|20 November}}. In his account, Morrell wrongly records the position of this anchorage, giving a location in open sea about {{convert|60|mi|-1}} south-west of the island's coastline.<ref name= WJM/> According to Morrell's account, ''Wasp'' then headed eastwards to hunt for seals, and reached the remote [[Bouvet Island]] on {{Nowrap|6 December}}. The polar historian [[Hugh Robert Mill]] notes that Morrell's description of this island's physical features fails to mention its most singular characteristic—the permanent ice sheet that covers its surface.<ref>H.R. Mill, pp. 106–07</ref><ref name= Morrell58>Morrell, pp. 58–62</ref> Morrell then attempted to take the ship southwards but, reaching thick ice at around 60°S, turned northeast towards the [[Kerguelen Islands]] where he anchored on {{Nowrap|31 December}}.<ref name= WJM/><ref name= Morrell58/>
[[Image:Bouvet island 0.jpg|thumb|left|alt= A low ice-covered island in blue choppy water, under a heavily clouded sky|[[Bouvet Island]], which Morrell claimed to have reached on 6 December 1822]]
After several days of exploration (and, evidently, profitable sealing), ''Wasp'' left the Kerguelens on {{Nowrap|11 January}} 1823, sailing south and east to record her furthest eastern position at 64°52'S, 118°27'E on {{Nowrap|1 February}}.<ref name= Morrell62>Morrell, pp. 62–65</ref><ref name= HRM107>H R Mill, pp. 107–08</ref> From this point, according to his own account, Morrell decided to take advantage of strong easterly winds, and made passage westward back to the [[Greenwich meridian]], 0°. His subsequent account of this voyage has been disputed, particularly his assertion that a distance of more than {{convert|3500|mi|km|sigfig=2}} was covered in 23 days.<ref name= Morrell62/> The writer [[Rupert Gould]] points out that, according to Morrell's record, this journey included a stretch of {{convert|900|mi|km}} in four days, a rate of progress that even Gould, generally sympathetic to Morrell, is inclined to doubt.<ref>Gould, p. 261</ref> Morrell quotes various positions during the voyage at southerly latitudes which later proved to be at least 100 miles inside the then undiscovered Antarctic continental mainland.<ref name= WJM/><ref name= HRM107/> One possible explanation for this discrepancy, offered by the writer W.J. Mills, is that since Morrell's account was written nine years after the voyage he may not have had access to the ship's log, and hence "felt constrained to invent details that appeared plausible", in order to sustain his narrative.<ref name= WJM/>

On {{Nowrap|28 February}}'', Wasp'' reached [[Candlemas Island]] in the South Sandwich Islands. After a few days spent in a search for fuel to feed the ship's stoves, Morrell sailed southwards on {{Nowrap|6 March}}, into the area later known as the Weddell Sea.<ref name= WJM/><ref>James Weddell, who first explored the area a month before Morrell, named the sea "King George IV's Sea". This name was not generally adopted; in 1900 the sea was formally named the Weddell Sea. Everett-Heath p. 409 (Weddell Sea entry)</ref> Finding the sea remarkably free of ice, Morrell advanced to 70°14'S before turning north-westward on {{Nowrap|14 March}}. This retreat, Morrell says, was due to the ship's lack of fuel; otherwise, he claims, in these open waters he could have taken the ship to 85°, or perhaps to the Pole itself.<ref name= Morrell66>Morrell, pp. 66–68</ref> These words are very similar to those used by the British explorer [[James Weddell]] to describe his own experiences in the same area, a month earlier, which has led historians to suspect that Morrell may have plagiarised Weddell's experiences.<ref>Simpson-Housley, p. 57</ref>

=== Sighting of land ===
[[Image:Morrell.jpg|thumb|upright|Engraving of Benjamin Morrell from 1832]]
From the earliest navigations of the Southern Ocean in the 16th century, lands which subsequently proved to be nonexistent had from time to time been reported.<ref>See list of reported lands and islands in: {{cite web|title= Non-existent islands (in Summary of Peri-Antarctic Islands)|url= http://www.spri.cam.ac.uk/resources/infosheets/19.html|publisher= Scott Polar Research Institute|year= 1996|access-date= 17 December 2008}}</ref> Robert Headland of the [[Scott Polar Research Institute]] has suggested various reasons for these false sightings, ranging from "too much [[rum]]" to deliberate hoaxes designed to lure rival ships away from good sealing grounds. Some sightings may have been of large ice masses that were carrying rocks and other [[moraine|glacial debris]]—dirty ice can appear convincingly similar to land. It is also possible that some of these lands existed, but later became submerged after volcanic eruptions. Other sightings may have been of actual land, the position of which was wrongly fixed through observational errors arising from chronometer failure, adverse weather or simple incompetence.<ref>Rubin, p. 152 (insert by Robert Headland: "Non-existent Antarctic Islands")</ref>

At 2 pm on 15 March, as ''Wasp'' cruised north-eastwards, Morrell records: "Land was seen from the masthead, bearing west, distance 3 leagues" (about nine miles, 14 km).<ref name= Morrell69>Morrell, pp. 69–70</ref> He did not at the time consider that he had made a new discovery; he seems to have assumed that he was seeing the east coast of the [[Antarctic Peninsula]], the western coast of which had been explored and given the name ''New South Greenland'' in 1821, by Robert Johnson, a former captain of the ''Wasp''.<ref name= WJM/> Johnson's name for this land was never adopted; in 1831 it was named [[Graham Land]].<ref>H R Mill, pp. 161–62.</ref> At the time of Morrell's voyage, the geographical character and dimensions of the peninsula were unknown; Morrell's recorded position was in fact far to the east of the peninsula.<ref>H R Mill, p. 109</ref> Morrell's account reads: "At half past {{Nowrap|4 pm}} we were close on with the body of land to which Captain Johnson had given the name of New South Greenland".<ref name= Morrell69/><ref>Simpson-Housley, map, p. 52</ref> The next few days were spent exploring this supposed coast, which was apparently rich in seal. Some {{convert|75|mi|km|sigfig=2}} further south, Morrell thought he could see snow-covered mountains.<ref name= Morrell69/>

After three days, Morrell called a halt "because of shortage of water and season far advanced".<ref name= Morrell69/> ''Wasp'' turned north, from a position Morrell calculated as 67°52'S, 48°11'W, and on {{Nowrap|19 March}}, the ship passed what he assumed was the northern cape of the land, at 62°41'S, 47°21'W. "This land abounds with oceanic birds of every description", wrote Morrell.<ref name= Morrell69/> He also records seeing 3,000 [[elephant seals|sea elephants]]. At 10 o'clock ''Wasp'' "bade farewell to the cheerless shores of New South Greenland",<ref name= Morrell69/> and sailed for [[Tierra del Fuego]], then through the [[Magellan Strait]] into the Pacific Ocean, reaching [[Valparaíso]], [[Chile]], on {{Nowrap|26 July}} 1823.<ref name= Morrell69/>

== Searches for Morrell's land ==
[[Image:1894 map of Antactica.jpg|thumb|left|alt= The upper of the two maps gives a projected outline of the then largely undiscovered coast of continental Antarctica, and shows its relations to the landmasses of South America, Africa and Australia. The lower map is an approximate representation of the Antarctic peninsula as envisaged in the late 19th century.|1894 maps of Antarctic regions showing the limited knowledge of Antarctic geography 70 years after Morrell. The lower map marks Ross's Appearance, but not New South Greenland]]
In 1838, the French explorer [[Jules Dumont d'Urville]] sailed over the position of Morrell's "north cape", but saw no indication of land.<ref name = Gould266>Gould, pp. 266–67</ref> This, together with the obvious errors in Morrell's voyage account, and his general reputation as a braggart, led most later geographers to doubt his story.<ref>H. R. Mill, pp. 104–05</ref> This scepticism remained even after Sir James Clark Ross reported an appearance of land in 1843, not far from Morrell's alleged observation; Ross's sighting was occasionally proffered as support for Morrell's claim.<ref name= Gould266/><ref>{{cite web|title= History of SANAE: chronological exploration|url= http://www.sanap.org.za/history.html|publisher= South African National Antarctic Programme|year= 2007|access-date= 17 December 2008|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080512122933/http://www.sanap.org.za/history.html |archive-date = May 12, 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> After Ross there was no further exploration of the Weddell Sea until 1903, when [[William Speirs Bruce]] took ''Scotia'' to 74°1'S, but in a sector of the sea which did not bring him close to Morrell's or Ross's supposed sightings.<ref>Speak, p. 92. Bruce reached his Farthest South at longitude 22°W.</ref> Bruce, however, did not dismiss Morrell's claims, writing that they should not be rejected until absolutely disproved.<ref>Gould, p. 271</ref>

The first determined search for New South Greenland came during the [[Second German Antarctic Expedition]], 1911–13, under Wilhelm Filchner. The expedition's ship, ''Deutschland'', became trapped in heavy sea ice while attempting to establish a shore base at [[Vahsel Bay]]. Her subsequent north-westerly drift had, by mid-{{Nowrap|June 1912}}, brought her to a position just {{convert|37|mi|km}} east of Morrell's recorded sighting.<ref name= Filch>{{cite web|title= Wilhelm Filchner 1877–1957|publisher= South-pole.com|url= http://www.south-pole.com/p0000103.htm|access-date= 18 December 2008}}</ref> Filchner left the ship on {{Nowrap|23 June}} and, with two companions and sufficient provisions for three weeks, sledged westward across the sea ice in search of Morrell's land. Daylight was limited to two or three hours a day, and temperatures fell to {{Convert|-35|C||abbr=}}, making travel difficult. They found no signs of land; a lead weight dropped through the ice reached a depth of {{convert|5248|ft|m}} before the line snapped. The depth confirmed that there was no land in the vicinity, and Filchner concluded that Morrell had probably seen a mirage.<ref name= Filch/>

On 17 August 1915 Sir Ernest Shackleton's ship ''Endurance'', trapped in the ice like ''Deutschland'' three years earlier, drifted to a point 10 miles west of Morrell's sighting. Here, a depth sounding recorded 1,676 fathoms (10,060 feet, 3,065 m), leading Shackleton to write: "I decided that Morrell Land must be added to the long list of Antarctic islands and continental coasts that have resolved themselves into icebergs".<ref name= Shack/> On {{Nowrap|25 August}} a further sounding of 1,900 fathoms (11,400 feet, 3,500 m) gave Shackleton additional evidence of the non-existence of New South Greenland.<ref name = Shack>Shackleton, pp. 60–61</ref>

Although Filchner's and Shackleton's investigations and observations were accepted as conclusive proof that New South Greenland was a myth,<ref>{{cite journal|title= New Land Found by Shackleton...New South Greenland a Myth|journal= New York Times|date= 2 June 1916|url= https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1916/06/02/100208096.pdf|access-date= 18 December 2008}}</ref> there remained the question of Sir James Ross's reported appearance of land in a position around 65°S, 47°W.<ref>Gould, p. 272</ref> Ross's reputation was sufficient for this possibility to be taken seriously, and for his alleged sighting to be recorded on maps and Admiralty charts.<ref>Wild, p. 91</ref> In 1922 [[Frank Wild]], leading the [[Shackleton–Rowett Expedition]] aboard ''Quest'' after Shackleton's death early in the expedition, investigated the location of Ross's sighting. Nothing was seen; prevented by ice conditions from reaching the exact spot, Wild took a sounding at 64°11'S, 46°4'W, which revealed {{convert|2331|fathom|ft m|0}} of water. This showed that no land was near.<ref>Wild, p. 144</ref>

== Opinions and theories ==
[[Image:Weddell Sea Iceberg.jpg|thumb|alt= High cliffs of an iceberg set in broken pack ice|Weddell Sea iceberg in the region of "New South Greenland", ''Endurance'' expedition August 1915. Shackleton observed how land appearances frequently resolved into icebergs.]]
Hugh Robert Mill, writing in 1905 before the non-existence of New South Greenland had been finally established, concluded that because of Morrell's blunders, and his habit of incorporating the experiences of others into his story, all his claims should be treated as unproven.<ref>H R Mill, p. 111</ref> Nevertheless, he conceded that "a man may be ignorant, boastful and obscure, and yet have done a solid piece of work".<ref>H. R. Mill, p. 105</ref> The Canadian geographer Paul Simpson-Housley, although sceptical about much of Morrell's account, suggests that the speeds claimed for the derided western journey, though fast, were not impossible,<ref name= Housley57>Simpson-Housley, pp. 57–69</ref> and Morrell's [[Farthest South|farthest south]] in the Weddell Sea, queried by Mill,<ref>H R Mill, p. 109.</ref> is entirely plausible, given that James Weddell had sailed four degrees further south just a month earlier.<ref name= Housley57/>

The writer [[Rupert Gould]], in a lengthy essay on New South Greenland published in 1929, queries the assumption that the sighting was simply invented by Morrell, partly on the grounds that very little weight is given to the discovery in Morrell's 500-page account. Gould writes: "If Morrell wished to gain an undeserved reputation as an Antarctic explorer, one would think he could have gone a better way about it than to bury his ''pièces justificatives'', after he had forged them, in an undistinguished corner of so bulky a book."<ref>Gould, p. 268</ref> Nor would he have credited it to Captain Johnson two years earlier, rather than to himself.<ref name= Housley57/>
[[Image:Approaching the Larsen Ice Shelf.jpg|thumb|left|alt= Aerial view of a range of icy mountains with a coastline visible in the foreground|The [[Larsen Ice Shelf]], on the eastern coast of the Antarctic peninsula]]
Gould also discusses the possibility that what Morrell sighted was the eastern coast of [[Graham Land]], the so-called "[[Foyn Coast]]",<ref>Gould uses the term "Foyn Coast" to describe the whole east coast of Graham Land. The Foyn Coast is actually only a short stretch of this coast, approximately {{convert|40|mi|km}} long, separated from the Weddell Sea by the [[Larsen Ice Shelf]]. See Stonehouse, p. 107</ref> despite its being 14° further west from the position of the New South Greenland sighting. Gould asserts that the features of the peninsula's eastern coast correspond closely with Morrell's description of New South Greenland.<ref>Gould, pp. 277–78</ref> This theory supposes that Morrell miscalculated the ship's position, perhaps because he lacked the chronometer necessary for proper navigational observation. In his account, Morrell writes that he was "destitute of the various nautical and mathematical instruments",<ref>Morrell, p. 67</ref> although other parts of his narrative seem to indicate that the occasional [[dead reckoning]] calculation was the exception to the norm.<ref>Gould, p. 276</ref> A longitudinal error of 14° is very large, and the additional distance of about {{convert|350|mi|km}} to the Foyn Coast seems too great to have been covered within the ten-day voyage from the South Sandwich Islands, where the ship's position is recorded accurately.<ref name= Housley57/> Even so, Gould suggests that a "balance of evidence" shows that what Morrell saw was the Foyn Coast.<ref>Gould, pp. 280–81</ref>
[[Image:2005-08-22 fata morgana.jpg|thumb|270px|alt= Distant shadowy appearances of land, seen across a wide expanse of sea|An example of a [[Fata Morgana (mirage)|Fata Morgana]], a form of [[superior mirage]], which distorts ice or distant coastlines so they might appear as islands with tall cliffs.]]
Filchner's view that the supposed sighting of New South Greenland could be explained by a mirage is echoed by Simpson-Housley. He suggests that Morrell and his crew saw a [[Mirage#Superior mirage|superior mirage]].<ref name= Housley57/> One form of superior mirage, sometimes described as a [[Fata Morgana (mirage)|Fata Morgana]], distorts distant flat coastlines or ice edges both vertically and horizontally, so they can appear to have tall cliffs and other features such as high mountain peaks and valleys.<ref>{{cite web|title= Arctic Climatology and Meteorology – Superior Mirage|url= http://nsidc.org/arcticmet/basics/phenomena/superior_mirage.html|publisher= National Snow and Ice Data Center|access-date= 19 December 2008|archive-date= 5 August 2011|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110805213027/http://nsidc.org/arcticmet/basics/phenomena/superior_mirage.html|url-status= dead}}</ref> In his expedition account ''South'', Shackleton gives a description of a Fata Morgana observed on {{Nowrap|20 August}} 1915, coincidentally as his ship ''Endurance'' drifted close to the recorded position of New South Greenland: "The distant pack is thrown up into towering barrier-like cliffs, which are reflected in blue lakes and lanes of water at their base. Great white and golden cities of Oriental appearance at close intervals along these cliff-tops indicate distant bergs ... The lines rise and fall, tremble, dissipate, and reappear in an endless transformation scene".<ref name="Shack"/>

== Afterwards ==
Morrell's four voyages finally ended on {{Nowrap|21 August}} 1831, with his return to New York.<ref>Morrell, p. 492</ref> He then wrote his ''Narrative of Four Voyages'', which was published the following year. He attempted to resume his seafaring career, seeking employment with the London-based shipping firm of Enderby Brothers, but his reputation had preceded him and he was rejected.<ref name= HRM/> Charles Enderby stated publicly that "he had heard so much of him that he did not think fit to enter into any engagement with him."<ref>Gould, p. 255</ref> Morrell also sought to join [[Dumont D'Urville]]'s expedition to the Weddell Sea in 1837, but his services were again declined.<ref name= HRM>H R Mill, pp. 110–11</ref> He reportedly died in 1839,<ref name= ANB>American National Biography (Vol. 15), p. 879</ref> and is commemorated by [[Thule Island|Morrell Island]], 59°27'S, 27°19'W, an alternative name for Thule Island in the [[Southern Thule]] sub-group of the South Sandwich Islands.<ref>{{cite web|title= South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands|url= http://www.geonames.org/search.html?country=GS&q=|publisher= Geonames|year= 2008|access-date= 19 December 2008}}</ref> Robert Johnson, who coined the name New South Greenland, disappeared with his ship in 1826, while investigating the Antarctic waters in the vicinity of what would later be known as the [[Ross Sea]].<ref name= HRM/><ref>{{cite web|title= History of the South Island of New Zealand (and adjacent islands) 1642–1835|url= http://www.nzetc.org/tm/scholarly/tei-McNMuri-t1-body-d1-d18.html#name-402465-mention|publisher= Victoria University of Wellington|year= 2008|access-date= 19 December 2008}}</ref>

Matsyn Island:
[[File:Blaeu 1645 - Regiones sub Polo Arctico.jpg|thumb|1645 map showing Willoughby's Land and Matsyn Island]]
During his 1553 voyage across the [[Barents Sea]], English explorer [[Hugh Willoughby]] thought he saw islands to the north. Based on his description, these islands were subsequently depicted and named "[[Willoughby's Land]]" and "'''Macsinof Island'''" on maps published by [[Petrus Plancius]] in 1592 and 1594 (although he was doubtful of their existence).<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hacquebord |first=Louwrens |date=Sep 1995 |title=In Search of ''Het Behouden Huys'': A Survey of the Remains of the House of Willem Barentsz on Novaya Zemlya |journal=Arctic |volume=48 |issue=3 |page=250 |url=http://pubs.aina.ucalgary.ca/arctic/Arctic48-3-248.pdf |accessdate=2009-03-08 |doi=10.14430/arctic1246 |archive-date=2009-03-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090327084815/http://pubs.aina.ucalgary.ca/arctic/Arctic48-3-248.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Gerardus Mercator]] included them on his [[:File:Merсator north pole 1595.jpg|1595 map]]. [[Willem Barentsz]] found no sign of Willoughby's discoveries and omitted them from his [[:File:Barentsz Full Map.jpg|map published in 1599]], but they continued to appear on Arctic maps published by [[Jan Janssonius]] and [[Willem Blaeu]] at least into the 1640s. Macsinof Island also appears as Macsin or Matsyn Island.

A theory propagated in 1612 held that Willoughby's Land was identical to [[Spitsbergen]], thus supporting an English claim prior to the Dutch discovery by Barentsz in 1596. This theory was used to justify a monopoly charter on whaling rights granted to the [[Muscovy Company]] in 1613.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hudson |first=Henry |authorlink=Henry Hudson |author2=Georg Michael Asher |title=Henry Hudson the Navigator: The Original Documents in which His Career is Recorded, Collected, Partly Translated, and Annotated |year=1860 |publisher=Hakluyt Society |location=London |pages=clix–clx |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_IwcVAAAAQAAJ |isbn=978-0-665-03626-2 }}</ref>

Asher (1860) believed the two islands to be merely a western transposition of the two islands of [[Novaya Zemlya]], and he saw a connection between Matsyn Island and "Matthew's Island," an early name for [[Severny Island]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Hudson |first=Henry |authorlink=Henry Hudson |author2=Georg Michael Asher |title=Henry Hudson the Navigator: The Original Documents in which His Career is Recorded, Collected, Partly Translated, and Annotated |year=1860 |publisher=Hakluyt Society |location=London |pages=clviii–clix |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_IwcVAAAAQAAJ |isbn=978-0-665-03626-2 }}</ref>

Royal Company's Islands:
[[Image:Nimrod.1909 voyage.jpg|thumb|right|1909 search for Royal Company and other phantom islands]]
[[File:Sud Polar Karte.jpg|right|thumb|1912 German map showing Royal Company Islands southwest of Tasmania]]
The '''Royal Company's Islands''' are a group of [[phantom island]]s reported by some early [[Exploration|explorers]] to lie southwest of [[Tasmania]].  They were first heard of before 1840, but the original report cannot be traced. Many old [[Map|charts]] show them at {{Coord|50|20|S|140|0|E|}} or {{Coord|52|20|S|143|0|E|}}.

The islands' existence was disproved as early as 1840 by the [[United States Exploring Expedition]].<ref>{{cite news |title=The Antarctic Continent |work=Hobart Courier |page=3 |date=Jan 12, 1841 |access-date=May 6, 2009 |quote=They sailed over the supposed place of the Royal Company's Islands, disproving their existence. |url=http://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/2957300 }}</ref>  From 1889 to 1902 several vessels passed through the islands' vicinity without noting any [[landform]]s, and in 1904 the [[UK Hydrographic Office]] finally decided to remove them from all [[Admiralty chart]]s.<ref>{{cite journal  |doi=10.1071/MU904032a  |date=July 1904 |title=Expunged Islands |journal=The Emu |volume=4 |pages=32 |url=http://www.publish.csiro.au/?act=view_file&file_id=MU904032.pdf |last1=Wharton |first1=W. J. L. }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=The Phantom Isles of the Pacific |work=New York Times |page=11 |date=May 15, 1904 |access-date=May 6, 2009 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1904/05/15/archives/the-phantom-isles-of-the-pacific-cruiser-tacoma-is-looking-for.html }}</ref>

In October 1894 the [[Antarctic_(ship)|'Antarctic']] ([[Henrik_Johan_Bull|H. Bull]]'s exploratory whaling expedition sponsored by [[Svend Foyn]]) steered for the Royal Company's Islands "supposed to be situated in about lat. 51 degrees S,. and long. 142 E.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Riffenburgh |first1=Beau |last2=Kløver |first2=Geir O. |title=Carsten Borchgrevinck and the Southern Cross, 1898-1900 |publisher=The Fram Museum |location=Oslo |isbn=978-82-8235-088-4 |page=152 |edition=1st}}</ref>" They searched for a couple of days, but met with gales. Not finding any islands, they headed for [[Macquarie Island]]. Further searches by the ''[[Nimrod (1867 ship)|Nimrod]]'' in 1909 and the ''[[SY Aurora|Aurora]]'' in 1912 turned up nothing.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Davis |first=J.K. |date=Dec 1910 |title=Voyage of the S. Y. "Nimrod.": Sydney to Monte Video Viâ Macquarie Island, May 8-July 7, 1909 |journal=The Geographical Journal |volume=36 |issue=6 |pages=696–703 |jstor=1776845|doi=10.2307/1776845 |publisher=Blackwell Publishing |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1449264 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=The Home of the Blizzard, being the story of the Australasian Antarctic expedition, 1911-1914 |last=Mawson |first=Douglas |author-link=Douglas Mawson |date=n.d. |publisher=Ballantyne Press |location=London |chapter=Chapter 18: The Ship's Story |chapter-url=http://www.coolantarctica.com/Antarctica%20fact%20file/History/Mawson_home_blizzard/mawson_blizzard_chapter18.htm |quote=Royal Company Islands not found in the position indicated on the chart }}</ref>

Keenan Land:
'''Keenan Land''' was the name given to a mass of land in the [[Beaufort Sea]] about 300 miles north of [[Point Barrow]], Alaska. It was allegedly discovered in the 1870s by American whaler John Keenan (1834/35, [[Watervliet, New York]] – March 11, 1910, [[Troy, New York]]).<ref>{{cite book |last=Mills |first=William James |title=Exploring Polar Frontiers: A Historical Encyclopedia |publisher=ABC-CLIO |year=2003 |isbn=1-57607-422-6 |page=72 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PYdBH4dOOM4C }}</ref>

John Keenan reported stranding his ship on an uncharted island, where he raised the American flag. After his return, the island was named after him.<ref>{{cite news |title=Capt. John Keenan |url=http://explorenorth.com/library/yafeatures/bl-keenan.htm |newspaper=The Troy Times |date=12 March 1910 |accessdate=11 June 2011}}</ref>

Starting in 1907 with the Anglo-American Polar Expedition, numerous unsuccessful attempts were made (by [[Vilhjalmur Stefansson]] and [[Roald Amundsen]], among others) to relocate Keenan Land. [[Hubert Wilkins]] flew over the area in 1937 on his search for the missing [[Sigizmund Levanevsky]] and came to the conclusion that the land never existed.

[[Image:Albino de Canepa 1489 Antillia Roillo.jpg|thumb|130px|Albino de Canepa, 1489. Showing "Roillo" right west of Antillia]]
'''Royllo''' (also '''Roillo'''), is a legendary [[phantom island]] that was once thought to be located in the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. It is probably identical with the island originally called '''Ymana''' in a 1424 [[nautical chart]] of [[Zuane Pizzigano]].  The island is usually depicted in many 15th-century maps as a small island located slightly to the west (20 [[League (unit)|leagues]] or so) of the much larger island of [[Antillia]].<ref>University of Minnesota, Twin Cities, "[http://bell.lib.umn.edu/map/PORTO/MYS/cort.html Armando Cortesão and Island Names]"</ref> It is often found in the group ''insulae de novo repertae'', or "newly discovered islands" along with other legendary islands.

Elizabeth Island (Cape Horn):
{{Short description|Phantom island in the South Atlantic}}
{{EngvarB|date=January 2014}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2014}}
[[File:Elizabeth Island.jpg|thumb|300px|[[Francis Fletcher (priest)|Francis Fletcher]]{{'s}} map of Elizabeth Island]]
'''Elizabeth Island''' is the name given to an island off the tip of South America
visited by [[Sir Francis Drake]] in September 1578, during [[Francis Drake's Circumnavigation|his circumnavigation]] of the globe.
The island was not seen again and is regarded as a [[Phantom island|phantom]]. Various suggestions have been offered as to where Drake landed.<ref name="Antarctic book">L. Ivanov and N. Ivanova. Phantom Islands. In: [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/364087925_The_World_of_Antarctica ''The World of Antarctica''.] Generis Publishing, 2022. pp. 74-77. {{ISBN|979-8-88676-403-1}}</ref>

==Background==
In 1578 Drake, with a small flotilla, was seeking to enter the Pacific to attack Spanish trade there. In August 1578, he arrived at the [[Straits of Magellan]]. By September he had found his way through and entered the [[Pacific Ocean]], only to be blown south in a series of storms. Parted from his consorts, Drake and his ship, [[Golden Hind|''Pelican'']], were at latitude 57°S (from [[Nuno da Silva (navigator)|Nuno da Silva]]; according to [[Richard Hakluyt]] "57 and a terce", i.e. 57°20') when, on 28 October, they encountered an island, and found shelter in a haven on its eastern shore.<ref name=FR>[[Felix Riesenberg]] ''Cape Horn''  Readers Union (1950)  ASIN: B0007J077K p54</ref>
Drake remained for three or four days, gathering wood and water, and "herbes of grete virtue", before setting out for the coast of South America.<ref name=FR/>

==Description==
The island was described by [[Francis Fletcher (priest)|Francis Fletcher]] (the expedition's chaplain) who left sketches and a map, and by da Silva, the navigator.
From this, marine historian [[Felix Riesenberg]] produced a composite: an island 30 miles from north to south, almost square, without a peak, with a lake at its centre; he hypothesised that it was the crater of an extinct volcano. He surmised a high shore, or cliff, on its southern shore, and a haven on the east. This place, named on later maps as Port Sir Francis Drake, was a sheltered harbour, with a depth of 20 [[fathom]]s and "a cannon shot" (about a mile) to the shore.<ref name="auto">Riesenberg p67</ref>
Fletcher also reported finding "plenty of the small berry which we named currants", and that he had left a memorial to Queen [[Elizabeth I]] with the date and year of their visit.<ref>Riesenberg p69</ref>

In a later account by [[Richard Hawkins]], Drake reported that he had made his way to the southernmost point of the island, and, stretching out over the edge, was able to claim that he had been "more further south than ... any man as yet known".<ref>Riesenberg p70</ref>

==Fate==
Elizabeth Island, and Port Sir Francis Drake, appeared on maps as late as that of [[Emanuel Bowen]] in 1747, but neither place was visited or seen again. 
Because of this, later writers have contended that Drake actually landed at [[Cape Horn]], from an account of the voyage – ''[[The World Encompassed]]'' – by Drake's nephew in 1628. However, Riesenberg points out that [[Hornos Island|Horn Island]] lacks wood, or fresh water, or a safe haven, or any other feature that Drake described,<ref>Riesenberg p68</ref> and offered an alternative suggestion. He notes that the position of the island is that of the [[Pactolus Bank]], a seamount rising to within {{Convert|70|fathom|metre|abbr=off}} of the surface, and suggests that the bank is the remnant of the island, disappeared in some volcanic eruption, or erosion by icebergs.<ref name="auto"/> The bank was discovered in 1885 by Capt. WD Burnham of the American ship ''Pactolus'', but more recent surveys have been unable to find the bank either, suggesting that it too may be a phantom island.{{fact|date=January 2020}} However historian [[Mateo Martinic]] considers [[Sars Bank]], 350 km south of [[Diego Ramírez Islands]], as a better fit for Elizabeth Island.<ref name=Martinic2019>{{cite journal |last1=Martinic B.|first1=Mateo |author-link1=Mateo Martinic |date=2019 |title=Entre el mito y la realidad. La situación de la misteriosa Isla Elizabeth de Francis Drake|trans-title=Between myth and reality. The situation of the mysterious Elizabeth Island of Francis Drake |url=https://scielo.conicyt.cl/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0718-22442019000100005&lng=es&nrm=iso&tlng=es |journal=[[Magallania]] |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=5–14 |doi=10.4067/S0718-22442019000100005 |access-date=December 21, 2019| language=es |doi-access=free }}</ref>  

Another [[Isabel Island (Chile)|Elizabeth Island]] in the [[Straits of Magellan]] was named and claimed for [[Kingdom of England|England]] by Drake on 24 August 1578.<ref>{{cite book |title=The World encompassed by Sir Francis Drake |last=Drake |first=Francis |author2=Francis Fletcher |year=1854 |publisher=Hakluyt Society |page=[https://archive.org/details/worldencompasse00vauxgoog/page/n131 75] |url=https://archive.org/details/worldencompasse00vauxgoog |display-authors=etal}}</ref> Further confusing the issue, the entire [[Tierra del Fuego]] [[archipelago]] was called the ''Elizabethides'' or Elizabeth Islands.{{fact|date=January 2020}}

Elizabeth Island would be significant as one of the first [[English overseas possessions|English territorial claims]] in the New World, preceding Drake's claim of [[New Albion]] in 1579 and [[Humphrey Gilbert]]'s claim of [[Colony of Newfoundland|Newfoundland]] in 1583.<ref>{{cite book |title=Sir Francis Drake |last=Sugden |first=John |year=1990 |publisher=Barrie & Jenkins |isbn=0-7126-2038-9 |page=118 }}</ref> Only [[Martin Frobisher]]'s claims in [[Baffin Island#History|Baffin Island]] (1576) and [[Greenland]] were earlier.<ref>{{cite book |title=Martin Frobisher: Elizabethan privateer |last=McDermott |first=James |year=2001 |publisher=Yale University Press |location=New Haven |isbn=0-300-08380-7 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/martinfrobishere0000mcde/page/190 190], 219 |url=https://archive.org/details/martinfrobishere0000mcde |url-access=registration }}</ref>
